**Direct answer:** No. WAL doesn't eliminate write contention. SQLite still allows only one writer at a time in WAL mode. What WAL adds is that readers and a writer no longer block each other, so reads and a write can run at the same time.

**Claims and sources**

- There can be only one writer at a time in WAL mode, so writers still contend with each other. The docs say: "since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time."
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- The concurrency benefit is that "readers do not block writers and a writer does not block readers. Reading and writing can proceed concurrently." SQLite also lists faster performance in most scenarios, more sequential disk I/O and fewer fsync() calls.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- The no-blocking property is only "mostly true." Some cases can still return SQLITE_BUSY, for example when another connection has the database open in exclusive locking mode. The docs say applications should be prepared for this.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

- WAL has costs. All processes must be on the same host, so it won't work over a network filesystem. If readers always overlap, checkpoints can't complete and the WAL file grows without bound.
  https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html

**Limits of the evidence**

- Everything comes from one source, the official SQLite WAL documentation. That is authoritative for this question, but it is not independent corroboration.
- My attempt to read a second SQLite page (the locking documentation) timed out. I found no source that disagrees, but I did not complete a counterevidence check.
- I did not verify how a second writer behaves when it hits the lock, such as the busy-timeout behavior. The page I read doesn't establish that, so I make no claim about it.

Sources:
- https://www.sqlite.org/wal.html
